newsitem.title: USA: Service Corp. says committed to Loewen deal.
newsitem.headline: Service Corp. says committed to Loewen deal.

text.p: Service Corp. International, North America's largest operator of funeral homes and cemeteries, said Wednesday it was committed to buying Loewen Group Inc. despite having been rebuffed by its smaller rival.
Houston-based Service Corp., which last week offered to buy Loewen in a friendly stock transaction valued at $2.8 billion, said it will hold a board meeting on Oct. 1 to consider its next move.
Industry analysts said they expected Service Corp. to launch a hostile takeover bid, perhaps as early as next week.

After meeting for about seven hours to discuss the offer, Loewen's board of directors late Tuesday unanimously rejected it, saying the unsolicited $43-a-share bid was inadequate and that it intended to remain an independent company.

"We are disappointed that the Loewen board of directors rejected our proposals without ever returning our calls or seeking more information from us. The actions of the Loewen board simply deprive its stockholders of the oppportunity to receive prompt value for their shares," Service Corp. Chairman Robert Waltrip said in a statement.

Service Corp. disclosed its offer last week and indicated it would be willing to raise the bid if Loewen granted it access to its financial records. The offer also calls for Service Corp. to assume about $1.3 billion of Loewen debt.
"I think (a hostile bid) looks fairly assured," said Kara Cheseby at the brokerage Legg Mason Wood Walker.
Service Corp. could not be reached for comment.

"I think (Service Corp.) ought to withdraw their offer and that will really anger the Loewen shareholders," said Todd Richter of Dean Witter. However, he acknowledged that Service Corp. is unlikely to walk away from the proposed transaction.
Instead, he speculated Service Corp. may try to lure Loewen shareholders by offering a higher price in a hostile offer.

Meanwhile, Loewen defended its decision and said it would not even be swayed by an offer as high as $52 a share. Analysts have speculated that Service Corp. could afford to pay as much as $50 a share without diluting its own earnings.

"I can't see any intellectual reason or rationale how the two could come together," Chief Executive Officer Raymond Loewen said in a telephone conference call. "I do not see any rational reason how they could ever acquire our company."
He also said Loewen's growth prospects were superior to Service Corp.'s, adding that this year's sales would exceed $900 million and would increase by about $300 million annually.

Analysts have said that Service might have a difficult time winning Loewen in a hostile bid because Raymond Loewen holds about 15 percent of the company's common shares and insiders hold about another 3 percent.
Service Corp. noted that its offer represented a 48.9 percent premium over the price Loewen stock was trading at 30 days before its offer.

"In addition, since Loewen stockholders would be receiving stock, they would continue to participate in Loewen's business as well as share in the upside of our business," said Service Corp. President William Heiligbrodt.
The belief that Service Corp. will pursue Loewen on a hostile basis comes mainly from its aggressive track record.

Service Corp. successfully wooed funeral firm Great Southern Group Plc of Britian two years ago despite an initial rejection. Service eventually paid $174.1 million for the British company after hiking its offer twice for Great Southern, which was holding talks with Loewen and another potential buyer.
Just a few weeks later it bought Plantsbrook Plc, also of Britain, for $290 million. The two acquisitions gave Service Corp. a 15 percent stake in the British funeral home market.
Shares of Loewen rose about 34 cents to $41.34 on Nasdaq. Service Corp. stock lost 50 cents to $29.50 on the New York Stock Exchange.
